strengths: Addresses a timely and real gap: existing controllable generation methods are either video-centric or audio-centric, and the paper is among the first to bring compositional multi-modal control (identity, timbre, pose, depth) into native joint audio-video DiT generation.

The technical design is sensible and well-motivated: the MMCU provides a unified interface for heterogeneous conditions, the Dual-Stream Bypass with zero-initialized output projectors preserves pretrained priors, and the auxiliary mask channel cleanly separates reference content from generation targets.

Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling is a practically useful feature, and the qualitative decoupled-control study (Fig. 7) convincingly demonstrates independent control of visual identity and acoustic timbre.
Training efficiency is notable: the frozen-backbone bypass approach trains in ~12 hours on 4 H200 GPUs over only 30k samples, making the approach accessible.

The evaluation is multi-faceted: quantitative comparisons on synchronization, identity, and structural fidelity (Tables 1-2), a human study with 20 participants (Table S1), and objective audio metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER).
As an Applied/Systems contribution, the system integration (two-stage progressive inference, distilled LoRA refinement, structured prompts via Qwen2.5-Omni) is competent and clearly described.
weaknesses: Missing ablation studies. There is no component-level analysis whatsoever: no ablation of the Dual-Stream Bypass vs. alternative injection schemes, the mask channel, bypass placement at even-numbered layers, control-dropout probability, or the contribution of modality-specific scaling quantitatively. For a paper claiming a new SOTA framework, this is a substantive evidentiary gap.

Comparison fairness is questionable. In Table 1, baselines (SadTalker, AniPortrait, Hallo3, HunyuanCustom) receive ground-truth audio and first frame while MMControl generates both from text; the authors acknowledge this asymmetry but still present headline metric wins as direct superiority. Moreover, no comparison is made against controllable joint audio-video models (e.g., variants of JavisDiT, MoCha in controllable settings), so the 'new state-of-the-art in controllable joint generation' claim is not established against like-for-like competitors.

The audio quality results (Table S2) lack baselines. SIM-o of 0.2574 is very low by zero-shot TTS standards (typically 0.6+), and SeedTTS-average WER of 17.58% is high, suggesting weak timbre fidelity and intelligibility. Without baseline numbers, it is impossible to judge whether these are acceptable for the task, which weakens the timbre-control claim.

Structural control is only quantitatively evaluated for depth (Table 2); pose control is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 6). A pose-adherence metric would substantially strengthen the structural-control claims.

Limited scope of the training data (a 30k subset of the Hallo3 talking-head dataset) restricts the system to single-speaker portrait/speech scenarios, while the framing suggests general joint audio-video control. Multi-character, non-speech, and scene-level audio cases are deferred to future work.
The evaluation benchmark is small (2×200 samples), self-constructed, and not stated to be released; combined with no code-release statement, reproducibility is a concern.

The Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling study (Fig. 7) only examines the binary values 0 and 1; a quantitative sweep over continuous γ values showing the fidelity-vs-quality trade-off claimed in Sec. 3.4 is absent.

Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially a ControlNet-style dual-branch adapter applied to a joint AV DiT with a mask-channel trick and per-modality guidance weights. This is acceptable for an Applied/Systems paper, but the components are individually well-known and the paper does not isolate what makes joint (rather than per-modality) conditioning effective.

No limitations or societal-impact discussion in the main text. For a system enabling controllable talking-person video with cloned voices, discussing misuse (deepfakes, voice cloning consent) would be expected.

strengths: Addresses a timely and genuinely under-explored problem: fine-grained multi-modal control (identity, timbre, pose, depth) within native joint audio-video DiTs, where prior work is either visual-centric or audio-centric.
The Multi-Modal Control Unit provides a clean, unified interface for heterogeneous conditions via temporal concatenation with binary masks, and the formulation (Eqs. 2-3) is clearly presented.

Engineering choices are sensible and well-motivated: bypass branches initialized from pretrained weights, zero-initialized output projectors for training stability, omission of cross-modal attention in branches for efficiency, and 12-hour fine-tuning demonstrating practical feasibility of adapting a large frozen backbone.

Offers both quantitative comparisons (VBench-style metrics, Sync-C/Sync-D, depth MAE) and a human study plus audio quality evaluation (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER) in the appendix, and a qualitative decoupled-control study of the guidance scaling factors.
Claim of highest Sync-C even against baselines using ground-truth audio is an interesting empirical observation supporting joint latent modeling.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially ControlNet/T2I-Adapter-style bypass injection plus reference-latent concatenation and mask channels applied to a joint audio-video backbone (LTX-2). Modality-specific guidance scaling is a straightforward extension of existing guidance/condition-strength knobs. No new training objective, architectural insight, or analysis is offered beyond straightforward adaptation.

Unfair baselines in Table 1: MMControl generates speech from text while all baselines use ground-truth audio and GT first frame. While framed as a 'harder task', this makes the quantitative comparison apples-to-oranges and the metrics favor the proposed method by construction; there is no joint audio-video baseline (e.g., JavisDiT, UniVerse, MoVA) even for unconditional generation quality.

Depth/pose control comparisons (Table 2) are against video-only methods (VideoComposer, ControlVideo, VACE) that were never designed for joint audio-video synthesis, so 'state-of-the-art in controllable joint generation' is supported by comparisons with methods that cannot perform the task.

Acoustic structural control is not actually implemented: the placeholder silence-latent design means pitch/energy contours are deferred to 'future extensions' (Section 3.2), weakening the claim of comprehensive multi-modal control.

Weak timbre evidence: the reported speaker similarity (SIM-o = 0.2574) is far below typical zero-shot TTS values and is reported without any baseline for context; timbre consistency, a central claim, is not quantitatively compared against any alternative.

Small and narrow training/eval scope: only 30k samples from the Hallo3 dataset (single-character talking heads), 200-sample self-constructed test sets, 20 participants for human evaluation, no statistical significance or variance reporting, and no ablations in the main paper isolating the contribution of the bypass design, mask channels, or two-stage inference.

Heavy reliance on a proprietary/external 19B backbone (LTX-2) including its distilled LoRA and upsampler; with no code or model release mentioned, reproducibility and attribution of gains (method vs. backbone quality) are unclear.

Missing limitations and societal-impact discussion despite obvious deepfake concerns (simultaneous identity and voice cloning of real people), which the venue explicitly values; the multi-character/conversational extension is acknowledged as unsolved but the single-speaker scope is understated elsewhere in the paper.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'establishes a new state-of-the-art in controllable joint generation' when no like-for-like joint-generation comparison exists, and 'perfectly synchronized' language in qualitative sections.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing joint audio-video generation models (LTX-2, JavisDiT, Sora 2, Veo 3) lack fine-grained controllability, and this paper is among the first to formalize Multi-Modal Controllable Joint Generation with composable visual, acoustic, and structural conditions.

The proposed framework is technically coherent: the MMCU provides a unified interface that tokenizes heterogeneous signals, the dual-stream bypass preserves the frozen LTX-2 prior (zero-initialized injection, weight inheritance from backbone embedders, mask-channel conditioning), and modality-specific guidance scaling (γv, γa) is a useful inference-time knob, as demonstrated in the decoupled control study (Fig. 7).

Evaluation is reasonably broad: quantitative comparisons on VBench-derived metrics, Sync-C/Sync-D, depth MAE, a human study with 20 participants across six criteria (Table S1), and an audio-quality evaluation with SIM-o, UTMOS, and WER (Table S2).
The training recipe is efficient and well documented (30K samples from Hallo3, 7,200 steps, ~12 hours on 4xH200, frozen backbone), which strengthens practical impact and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core mechanism is essentially a ControlNet/VACE-style bypass adapter extended to a joint AV DiT, and reference-image conditioning via latent prepending with binary masks closely follows established first-frame/customization paradigms (e.g., Wan-S2V, Phantom, SkyReels-A2). Modality-specific guidance scaling is a simple scalar reweighting. The paper would benefit from positioning against these closely related adaptation techniques and from a stronger articulation of what is fundamentally new.

Comparisons are weak on the most relevant axis: no comparison against joint audio-video generation or audio-driven character models that could also accept references (e.g., MoCha, JavisDiT, Universe-1, Wan2.2-S2V). Table 1 compares against cascaded portrait-animation methods that use ground-truth audio and first frames, and the authors themselves acknowledge this task asymmetry; the claimed SOTA in 'controllable joint generation' is therefore not directly established against a like-for-like joint baseline.

Missing quantitative ablations: there is no ablation of the bypass branch design (e.g., with/without modality-specific branches, mask channels, layer placement), the two-stage inference strategy, or dropout/CFG choices. The γv/γa study is purely qualitative. For an algorithm contribution, component-wise evidence is important.

Pose control has no quantitative evaluation: structural control is quantified only for depth; the pose experiments (Fig. 6) are qualitative only, despite pose being listed as a headline capability. A pose-alignment metric (e.g., pose estimation error on generated videos) is expected.

The audio evaluation raises concerns: SIM-o of 0.2574 is very low compared to typical zero-shot TTS speaker-similarity scores (>0.6), and WER (17.58% SeedTTS avg) is high; both are reported without baselines or discussion of whether the joint model limits timbre fidelity. The claim of 'timbre-consistent audio' is not well supported by these numbers.

Depth-MAE comparison in Table 2 is against video-only models (VideoComposer, ControlVideo, VACE) that do not jointly generate audio; the comparison conflates differences in task and backbone scale (VACE is not built on a 19B joint AV model).
Reproducibility is uncertain: no code, model, or benchmark release is mentioned, and the evaluation benchmark (200+200 samples) is newly constructed without a stated release plan.

Minor: some references appear inconsistent or likely erroneous (e.g., 'Team et al., 2026' / MOVA arXiv IDs dated 2026), and the abstract/intro use strong SOTA language that the evidence only partially supports.

strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap: existing controllable generation methods target either video-only or audio-only conditions, while native joint audio-video DiTs lack a unified fine-grained control mechanism. The formulation of Multi-Modal Controllable Joint Generation is well motivated.

The technical design is coherent and practical: the MMCU provides a clean unified tokenization of heterogeneous controls (reference image, reference audio, depth/pose) with binary masks; the Dual-Stream Bypass follows established ControlNet-style principles (trainable branches, zero-initialized output projection, weight inheritance from the frozen backbone) adapted sensibly to a joint AV DiT; modality-specific guidance scaling (γv, γa) is a simple but useful inference-time control knob.

Experimental evidence is reasonably broad: comparisons against audio-driven baselines (SadTalker, AniPortrait, HunyuanCustom, Hallo3) and structural-control baselines (VideoComposer, ControlVideo, VACE, Text2Video-Zero), a benchmark with Sync-C/Sync-D, CLIP/DINO identity metrics, depth and pose MAE, plus human evaluation, audio quality metrics (SIM-o, UT MOS, WER), and a component ablation (Table S3) that substantiates each design choice (masks, weight inheritance, dual-stream vs. unified attention, skipping cross-attention in branches).

Comparison with the concurrent AVControl framework (Table S5) and honest reporting of cases where baselines win (e.g., Hallo3's higher Dynamic Degree, AVControl's higher aesthetic quality in pose setting) increase credibility.
Training is efficient (7.2k steps, ~12 hours on 4 H200s) by keeping the 19B backbone frozen, which is a practical advantage and makes the approach reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a ControlNet/T2I-Adapter-style bypass adapted to LTX-2, with mask-channel concatenation and a scalar gate on the residual hint. The formalization (Eqs. 1-5) is straightforward, and the guidance-scaling mechanism reduces to independent scaling of residual hints. The contribution is primarily an engineering integration rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Training data is only 30k curated samples from Hallo3, which is a talking-head/portrait dataset. This raises concerns about domain generality: claims of general joint audio-video controllable generation are supported mostly by single-character, speech-centric talking-head scenarios. The paper itself concedes multi-character, conversational settings and long-horizon coherence are left to future work, but the abstract and claims do not sufficiently scope this limitation.

Fairness of the main comparison (Table 1) is questionable: baselines use ground-truth audio and the first GT frame, while MMControl generates both modalities from text. The authors acknowledge this asymmetry, but it means the reported wins (Sync-C, Text CLIP, DINO) are not like-for-like. Moreover, there is no quantitative comparison against native joint AV generation models (e.g., LTX-2 itself without control, JaviDiT), which would be the most relevant reference point for the claimed gap.

Timbre control appears weak in absolute terms: SIM-o of 0.2574 is quite low compared to typical zero-shot TTS speaker similarity (often 0.6+), and Table S2 reports only absolute values with no baseline, making it hard to judge how effective the acoustic control actually is.

The self-constructed benchmark (200 samples per task) is small, drawn presumably from the sameHallo3-derived distribution as training data, and details on test-set construction and information-leakage prevention are thin. VBench results are mentioned in the setup but never reported. No code or model release is stated, limiting reproducibility and independent verification.

Some analyses are only qualitative (decoupled control study in Fig. 7 uses only extreme γ values 0/1; Table S4 is limited), and the interplay between γ scaling and CFG is not analyzed. Missing discussion of failure cases and compute/latency cost of bypass branches at inference.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: bringing fine-grained multi-modal control (identity, timbre, depth/pose) into joint audio-video DiT generation, rather than the well-studied video-only or audio-driven talking-head settings.

The system design is reasonable and clearly described: the MMCU unifies heterogeneous control signals with binary masks, the Dual-Stream Bypass follows a sensible ControlNet-style recipe (frozen backbone, weight-inherited projectors, zero-initialized output projection), and modality-specific guidance scaling is a useful inference-time knob.

Experimental coverage is broad: quantitative comparisons across audio-driven baselines and structural-control baselines, a user study, audio-quality metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER), component ablations (Table S3), guidance-scaling ablations (Table S4), and a comparison with a concurrent framework (AVControl).

Training is efficient (30k samples, ~12 hours on 8 H200s) by reusing a pretrained LTX-2 backbone, which is practical and reproducible in spirit, and implementation details are reported at a reasonable level.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear task definition and honest acknowledgment of limitations (single-character, conversational settings left to future work).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The contribution is essentially a well-executed assembly of established techniques (ControlNet/T2I-Adapter-style bypass branches, reference-latent conditioning with mask channels, zero-init projections, CFG-like guidance scaling) applied to a new backbone. The paper would benefit from articulating what is scientifically non-obvious about extending these to joint AV diffusion.

Comparisons are structurally unfair. Against audio-driven baselines (Hallo3, SadTalker, AniPortrait), MMControl consumes the text prompt while baselines use ground-truth audio and the first frame; against a 19B pretrained joint AV backbone, these much smaller talking-head models are not comparable. Crucially, the paper does not compare against other joint AV generation models (e.g., JavisDiT, Universe) on generation quality, which is the core setting it claims to advance.

Evaluation is on a self-constructed benchmark (200-sample sets) with metrics computed by the authors' own preprocessing pipeline (e.g., depth/pose MAE from their own extracted signals), which can favor their method; no standard public benchmark is used, and some compared visual-control baselines (VideoComposer, ControlVideo, Text2Video-Zero) are dated (2023).

The audio-quality results are presented without baselines: SIM-o of 0.2574 is quite low as a speaker-similarity score, and Table S2 reports only MMControl's numbers, making it impossible to judge whether timbre control is actually competitive. Similarly, the claimed timbre-preservation benefit is not directly compared against, e.g., cascaded TTS+video pipelines.

Clarity and rigor gaps: Eq. (5) is described as a 'gated' residual but is written as a simple scaled sum, and the dimensional notation is loose; details such as how the reference-audio duration k is chosen, temporal alignment between audio and video latents, and how failure cases behave are missing.
The decoupled control study (Fig. 7) is purely qualitative; a quantitative matrix over (γ_v, γ_a) would substantiate the central 'independent control' claim, which is the paper's headline feature.
Societal impact is under-addressed: a system generating identity- and voice-faithful talking videos of reference persons has obvious deepfake risks; the paper offers no discussion or safeguards.
Some references appear incomplete or implausible (future-dated entries, 'accessed 2026'), and figure resolutions (Figs. 2-3) are too small to parse, which weakens presentation quality.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing controllable-generation methods (ControlNet/T2I-Adapter-style bypasses, customization frameworks) target visual-only generation, while native joint audio-video DiTs lack fine-grained multi-modal conditioning. Framing 'Multi-Modal Controllable Joint Generation' as a task, and unifying identity, timbre, and structure controls, is a meaningful contribution.

The Dual-Stream Bypass architecture is a sensible and well-motivated design: frozen joint DiT backbone with parallel trainable branches, modality-specific context projectors with weight inheritance, mask channels to distinguish reference from generation, and zero-initialized output projection. The deliberate omission of cross-modal attention inside the bypass branches is a thoughtful choice, and it is validated by ablation (B4).

The evidence base is reasonably thorough for a systems-style contribution: quantitative comparisons against audio-driven baselines (SadTalker, AniPortrait, HunyuanCustom, Hallo3) and structural-control baselines (VideoComposer, ControlVideo, VACE, Text2Video-Zero), a comparison with the concurrent AVControl framework, a user study with 20 participants over six criteria, objective audio-quality metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER), and a component ablation covering masks, weight inheritance, and each bypass stream.

The modality-specific guidance scaling (γ_v, γ_a) provides practical inference-time control without retraining; the guidance-scaling ablation (Table S4) and the decoupled-control qualitative study (Fig. 7) demonstrate that visual identity and acoustic timbre can be steered independently, which is the paper's central claim.

Training cost is modest (30k samples, ~12 hours on 8 H200s, frozen backbone), which makes the approach attractive and reproducible relative to training joint generators from scratch, and the method is compatible with the LTX-2 two-stage inference pipeline.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a concern. In Table 1, the audio-driven baselines are given ground-truth audio and the ground-truth first frame, while MMControl generates both from text plus references. The paper acknowledges this but still claims superiority; the settings are not equivalent, and the baselines are portrait-animation systems evaluated on a self-constructed 200-sample benchmark drawn from Hallo3 data that favors MMControl's training distribution. A comparison against strong joint AV or audio-to-video systems (e.g., LTX-2 itself, MoCha, Wan2.2-S2V, JavisDiT) is missing from the main results.

The reported speaker similarity of 0.2574 (SIM-o, Table S2) is unusually low—modern zero-shot timbre-control systems typically report substantially higher values on comparable protocols. Either the metric is being computed in an unconventional way (e.g., generated vs. generated audio rather than vs. reference), or timbre control is weak; the paper does not contextualize this number against any reference point, which undermines the 'timbre-consistent audio' claim.

The task definition emphasizes general joint audio-video scene generation, but the data (Hallo3 subset, 30k clips of segmented characters) and all qualitative examples are essentially single-character talking-head/portrait scenarios. The paper should more honestly scope its contribution to portrait-style generation; the depth and pose tasks partially mitigate this but follow the same narrow data regime, and evaluation of general scenes (VBench results are mentioned but never reported in the tables shown).

Evidence quality issues reduce confidence in the quantitative claims: benchmarks are self-constructed (200 samples each) with no public release stated; several headline tables contain small inconsistencies (e.g., MMControl loses on Subject DINO to VACE and ControlVideo in the pose task, in Dynamic Degree in Table 3, and Motion Smoothness to Hallo3 in Table 1, which are downplayed); and the abstract/conclusion use 'state-of-the-art' language that overstates what a single-domain, 200-sample evaluation supports.

The method is architecturally incremental: MMCU, bypass branches with zero-init projection, weight inheritance, and guidance scaling are all well-established patterns (ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, IP-Adapter-style conditioning) adapted to the joint AV DiT setting. The novelty lies in the combination and application rather than a new technique, which limits the conceptual contribution unless the unified multi-modal control demonstration is deemed sufficiently important.

Some exposition is imprecise: Eq. 5 describes γ_v and γ_a as 'adaptively' modulating influence, but they are user-set scalars; the appendix reports metrics on differing sample counts across tables (90, 60, 150, 200), complicating cross-table comparison; and future-work limitations (multi-character, long-horizon coherence) are noted but not accompanied by discussion of current failure modes.
